# Material and Methods
The methodology of this thesis is structured around two primary phases. The first phase establishes the underlying ecological algorithm, detailing the data processing and statistical pipeline required to generate a wild boar resistance surface. The second phase focuses on translating this conceptual workflow into an applied software solution through the development of an automated, user-facing QGIS plugin. Together, these sections outline both the ecological logic required to model habitat connectivity and the software engineering steps used to package this pipeline into a functional tool.

## Software Environment and Data Inputs
This section details the computational tools and empirical datasets required to construct the resistance surface pipeline and develop the automated QGIS tool. It outlines the programming frameworks utilized for geoprocessing, as well as the specific biological and spatial datasets necessary to calibrate and verify the underlying ecological model.

### Development Environment
The development of the resistance surface pipeline and the subsequent QGIS plugin required a dual-language software environment, utilizing both R and Python.

The ecological algorithm, encompassing the step-selection analysis and initial model calibration, was developed in R (version 4.5.1). Spatial data handling and vector operations were executed using the terra (version 1.9.11) and sf (version 1.1.0) packages, while movement ecology metrics and track resampling were processed with amt (version 0.3.1.0). Extensive data wrangling and temporal operations were performed using dplyr (version 1.2.1), tidyr (version 1.3.1), purrr (version 1.1.0), and lubridate (version 1.9.4). The integrated step-selection function was fitted via conditional logistic regression using the survival package (version 3.8.3), with model outputs standardized using broom (version 1.0.10). Visualizations of the statistical outputs were generated with ggplot2 (version 4.0.3).

The automated tool was implemented as a plugin for QGIS version 3.40.13. The plugin’s backend geoprocessing logic and graphical user interface (GUI) were written in Python [Insert Python Version]....

### Calibration and Testing Data
To delineate the spatial extent of the study, administrative boundaries were extracted from the tlm_kantonsgebiet layer of the swissBOUNDARIES3D dataset. Canton Aargau served as the primary training area to calibrate the ecological resistance model, whereas Canton Zürich was designated as the independent transfer area to evaluate the automated QGIS tool. To mitigate spatial edge effects during the geoprocessing phases, a geometric buffer of 2,000 meters was initially applied around the cantonal perimeters. The resulting geometry was then converted into a rectangular bounding box utilizing the st_as_sfc function.

Because the high-resolution environmental covariates utilized in this project are inherently restricted to the Swiss national territory, this rectangular extent was subsequently cropped at the national boundary. The overarching ecological and analytical pipeline of this thesis—including the deliberate reliance on highly detailed national datasets—was strongly guided by the methodological framework established in the comprehensive red deer connectivity study by Fischer et al. (2024).

While Canton Aargau shares a direct northern border with Germany, extending the study area into German territory was explicitly excluded from the experimental design. Although it is technically feasible to combine Swiss topographical and land-cover data with corresponding German datasets, undertaking such a cross-border harmonization would have vastly exceeded the scope of this project. Integrating international geodata necessitates the complex standardization of disparate semantic classifications (e.g., reconciling swissTLM3D categories with German ATKIS data), native spatial resolutions, and coordinate reference systems.

Alternatively, utilizing seamless pan-European (e.g., CORINE Land Cover) or global datasets to circumvent the border issue was considered but ultimately rejected. Employing these international datasets would have drastically decreased the spatial and thematic accuracy of the model. Transnational datasets typically operate at much coarser resolutions (often 100 meters or more) and feature highly generalized land-cover classifications. They fail to capture critical micro-habitat structures, such as narrow forest corridors, minor roads, or small-scale anthropogenic features. Because the step-selection function in this study relies on high-frequency, 15-minute GPS telemetry, matching these precise animal movement steps with coarse environmental data would have fundamentally undermined the biological validity of the resulting resistance surface. It is for this exact reason that the decision was made to restrict the study area strictly to the Swiss border, accepting the methodological trade-off of edge effects in favor of maximizing local data accuracy and resolution.

To ensure strict spatial alignment across all pipeline outputs within this defined perimeter, a master raster grid was generated. This grid was standardized to the Swiss coordinate reference system LV95 (EPSG:2056) with a uniform spatial resolution of 25 meters. Finally, to optimize computational efficiency, the geometry of the buffered study area was converted into a Well-Known Text (WKT) string. WKT is a standardized text markup language that represents complex vector geometries, such as polygons, as compact and highly readable text strings. Passing this lightweight format directly into the spatial processing libraries drastically reduces computational overhead, serving as a rapid spatial filter to significantly accelerate the loading and masking of the large environmental covariate datasets.


#### Wild Boar Telemetry Data
The biological foundation of the model consisted of an extensive GPS telemetry dataset of wild boars (Sus scrofa), collected by the Wildlife Management Research Group (WILMA, ZHAW) as part of the "Wildschweinschreck" project. Between 2014 and 2017, a total of 36 individuals were equipped with GSM-GPS tracking collars (VECTRONIC Aerospace) within the Aargau study areas of Elfingen and Felsenau. The devices were programmed to record a spatial location point at a standard interval of 15 minutes.

The primary methodological benefit of integrating this specific dataset was that it enabled a strictly empirical approach to modeling the resistance surface. Rather than defining landscape permeability based on subjective expert knowledge (expert opinion), the high-frequency GPS data allowed for the calculation of a data-driven Step-Selection Function (SSF). This approach ensured that the final resistance values objectively reflected the actual, quantifiable movement behavior of the animals, thereby providing a robust scientific foundation for the QGIS tool.

Regarding data quality, however, the original data file exhibited considerable complexity and heterogeneity. The raw dataset contained a multitude of semantic annotations (such as sun and moon phases, or distances to forest edges), many of which were not retained for the current pipeline. A significant limitation was the incomplete temporal coverage of certain attributes; for example, data regarding agricultural crops (the "Frucht" column) were only systematically recorded sporadically during specific field surveys in the summer months. Furthermore, the temporal intervals (timestamps) between the GPS points showed irregularities due to signal loss or collar disconnections. The detailed preprocessing steps undertaken to clean these incomplete attributes and regularize the timestamps are discussed extensively in the subsequent chapter [Insert cross-reference to your Quarto chapter: Telemetry Processing and Step Classification].


#### SwissBOUNDARIES3D
To delineate the precise spatial extent of the study areas, the swissBOUNDARIES3D dataset (version 1.5) was utilized. Provided by the Federal Office of Topography (swisstopo) , this comprehensive vector dataset contains the administrative boundaries and territorial units of Switzerland in a three-dimensional format. Specifically, the dataset defines its geometries as a sequence of three-dimensional coordinates (x, y, z), which is achieved by projecting the administrative borders onto the highly accurate digital elevation model swissALTI3D. For this project, the dataset was implemented in the GeoPackage format, standardized to the Swiss coordinate reference system LV95 (LN02).

The primary benefit of utilizing swissBOUNDARIES3D lies in its design as a foundational reference dataset, making it ideal for spatial analyses that require an exact integration with other national geodatasets. The dataset features a homogeneous, nationwide quality and guarantees a high geometric accuracy of $\pm0.5$ meters in both position and elevation. This precision is continuously verified and improved through the integration of original data from official cadastral surveying. Within the geoprocessing pipeline, the specific polygon feature class TLM_KANTONSGEBIET  was targeted to accurately extract the administrative geometries of Canton Aargau (serving as the training extent) and Canton Zürich (serving as the transfer extent).

Despite its exceptional technical quality, relying on this dataset introduces a specific ecological limitation: administrative boundaries are political constructs that rarely align with natural topography or continuous wildlife habitats. To mitigate this limitation and prevent abrupt boundary cut-offs from causing artificial edge effects in the resistance model, the geometries extracted from swissBOUNDARIES3D were not used as hard limits. Instead, they were buffered by 2,000 meters to capture the necessary ecological transition zones surrounding the targeted cantons before being converted into a rectangular processing extent.


#### SwissTLM3D
To represent the complex spatial configuration of land cover and anthropogenic infrastructure, the Topographic Landscape Model of Switzerland, swissTLM3D (2026 edition), was incorporated into the modeling pipeline. Provided by the Federal Office of Topography (swisstopo), this comprehensive vector geodatabase served as the primary source for deriving environmental covariates. The dataset was utilized in the GeoPackage format and standardized to the LV95 coordinate reference system.

The primary benefit of employing swissTLM3D was its immense thematic depth and high spatial accuracy, which allowed for the targeted extraction of specific landscape elements known to dictate wild boar movement and habitat selection. To construct the resistance surface, the raw data was filtered into functionally distinct ecological categories. To model protective cover and primary habitats, natural vegetation classes—specifically closed forest ("Wald"), open forest ("Wald offen"), scrub ("Gebueschwald"), and woody areas ("Gehoelzflaeche")—were extracted. Conversely, land-use types that act as barriers, are subject to intense management, or fail to provide consistent cover were explicitly excluded from the available habitat matrix. These exclusions comprised unstocked forests ("Wald nicht bestockt"), mining areas ("Abbauareal"), orchards ("Obstanlage"), cemeteries ("Friedhof"), vineyards ("Reben"), and water bodies ("Gewässerareal").

The dataset was equally crucial for mapping the structural variables that increase landscape resistance. The highly differentiated road network was classified into three distinct categories based on expected barrier effects and mortality risks: fenced highways and high-speed infrastructure (e.g., "Autobahn", "Autostrasse", "Einfahrt"), main roads (e.g., "10m Strasse", "8m Strasse"), and secondary or access roads (e.g., "4m Strasse", "3m Strasse"). Furthermore, anthropogenic disturbance zones were mapped using the tlm_namen_siedlungsname polygon layer, combining built-up areas across multiple scales, from entire towns ("Ort") down to sub-neighborhoods ("Quartierteil") to ensure full coverage of settlement boundaries.

A defining quality feature of swissTLM3D that heavily benefited the spatial processing was the inclusion of the Kunstbaute (artificial structure) attribute. This attribute enabled a highly specific filtering step: linear infrastructure features located below ground level or enclosed within structures—such as tunnels ("Tunnel"), underpasses ("Unterführung"), or roads inside buildings ("in Gebäude")—were systematically identified and removed from the surface layer. This vital preprocessing step ensured that subterranean infrastructure, which is physically invisible to wild boars, did not artificially inflate above-ground resistance values in the final model.

Despite its exceptional cartographic quality, relying on swissTLM3D for ecological modeling presented certain limitations. The dataset represents a static, generalized snapshot of the landscape. It inherently lacks temporal dynamics, meaning it cannot account for seasonal variations highly relevant to wild boar ecology, such as the shifting presence of agricultural crops (e.g., maize) or temporary human activity. Additionally, the strict semantic categorizations are designed for topographical mapping rather than biology; a polygon classified simply as "Wald" does not quantify the density of the understory, forcing the spatial algorithm to assume a uniform habitat quality across all broadly classified forest features.

#### DHM25
To establish the topographical foundation of the wild boar resistance surface, the Digital Height Model DHM25 (dhm25_grid_raster.asc) was incorporated into the spatial pipeline. Sourced from the Federal Office of Topography (swisstopo), the DHM25 is a comprehensive grid model that represents the three-dimensional shape of the earth's surface, specifically excluding vegetation and built structures. The dataset was utilized in its native ASCII grid format, featuring a uniform spatial resolution of 25 meters and originally referenced to the Swiss LV03 coordinate system (EPSG:21781).

The primary benefit of utilizing the DHM25 for this tool-development project was its seamless alignment with the study's target macroscopic spatial scale. Because the final master grid of the resistance surface was purposefully designed with a 25-meter resolution, the DHM25 provided a perfectly scaled topographical baseline out of the box. This allowed for the rapid, computationally efficient derivation of critical geomorphological covariates—such as terrain slope and the Topographic Ruggedness Index (TRI)—which were assumed to influence wild boar energy expenditure and movement. Utilizing this pre-rasterized 25-meter model avoided the severe computational overhead that would have been required to aggregate and downsample modern, ultra-high-resolution LiDAR datasets (such as swissALTI3D) across multiple cantonal extents.

Regarding data quality, the DHM25 is built upon a robust historical foundation, having been derived from the digitized contour lines and specific spot heights of the official Swiss National Map 1:25,000. Its vertical accuracy remains highly reliable for macroscopic ecological modeling, though it varies systematically depending on the terrain's complexity. The model achieves an average height accuracy of $\pm1.5$ meters in the relatively flat Swiss Plateau (Mittelland), scaling to $\pm3$ to $\pm8$ meters in the steep Alpine and Prealpine regions.

However, the application of this dataset introduced distinct methodological limitations. Most notably, the DHM25 is considered a legacy dataset, as its fundamental altitude data was primarily surveyed between 1952 and 1979, with final updates concluded in 1999. Consequently, significant recent terrain alterations—such as modern highway earthworks, large-scale quarry expansions, or newer noise-protection embankments—are not reflected in the topography. Furthermore, because it is strictly a "bare-earth" digital terrain model, it inherently lacks any data regarding the height or density of the forest canopy. To compensate for this limitation and adequately model the protective cover that is vital to wild boar habitat selection, it was strictly necessary to fuse the DHM25 data with the current land-cover polygons provided by the swissTLM3D dataset.

#### Wildlife Passages
To specifically address points of localized permeability across major anthropogenic barriers, the national geodatabase of wildlife passages (Wildtierpassagen.gdb) was integrated into the spatial model. Issued by the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN), this vector dataset catalogs the locations and operational status of dedicated wildlife crossing structures across Switzerland. For this study, the specific polygon layer N2023_Version_Wildtierpassagen (representing the 2023 update) was utilized, formatted in the LV95 coordinate reference system.

The primary benefit of employing this targeted dataset was its capacity to correct artificial barrier effects generated by the swissTLM3D road network. In a baseline raster model, a fenced highway is typically calculated as an absolute, continuous barrier. By overlaying the polygons of functional wildlife passages, these crossing points could be explicitly programmed into the QGIS plugin as high-conductivity corridors, allowing the modeled resistance to accurately drop back to zero at these specific locations. This ensures that the simulated connectivity pathways realistically reflect the actual movement opportunities available to wild boars, rather than being falsely truncated by continuous infrastructure lines.

The data quality of the FOEN wildlife passages is generally robust, as the geometries are precisely mapped at a scale of 1:25,000 and the dataset provides detailed attribute information regarding the construction status and functionality of each crossing. This allowed for the methodological exclusion of planned or defunct passages, ensuring that only actively functional structures were integrated as permeable pixels in the current resistance surface.

However, a notable limitation of this dataset is its thematic restriction to dedicated wildlife crossing structures (e.g., green bridges or specialized underpasses). It does not comprehensively map multi-use infrastructure that wild boars frequently exploit for movement, such as agricultural underpasses, large drainage culverts, or unlit forestry bridges. Consequently, while the dataset successfully opens major, state-sanctioned corridors across highways, the final resistance surface likely still underestimates the true, fine-scale permeability of the landscape where opportunistic, undocumented crossing structures exist.

#### Permanent Fences Canton Zürich
To incorporate hard anthropogenic obstacles into the landscape matrix of the canton Zürich, a dedicated vector dataset of permanent fences (Dauerzäune.shp) was utilized. Sourced from the Cantonal Veterinary Office (Veterinäramt), this shapefile delineated extensive permanent fencing structures constructed primarily as preventive barriers against the spread of African Swine Fever (ASP). The dataset consisted of high-resolution Polygon geometries representing the exact spatial extent of these installations across the landscape.

The primary methodological benefit of integrating this dataset was its application as an absolute spatial barrier within the resistance model. In standard landscape modeling, favorable land cover or flat topography might inherently calculate as a highly permeable corridor; however, the presence of a permanent, wildlife-proof fence physically halts wild boar movement entirely. By incorporating and rasterizing these features, the geoprocessing algorithm could explicitly assign maximum resistance (zero permeability) to these specific pixels. This step effectively overrode the underlying habitat suitability derived from the broader environmental layers, such as swissTLM3D and DHM25, ensuring the final surface reflected true on-the-ground impassability.

Regarding data quality, the shapefile provided a robust, officially verified mapping of significant, permanent defensive structures. However, a notable limitation of this dataset was its strict exclusivity to major, state-documented fences. It inherently did not account for temporary agricultural fencing, localized forestry enclosures for sapling protection, or unmapped private property boundaries. Consequently, while the dataset successfully closed off major artificial corridors within the model, the final resistance surface inevitably omitted some smaller-scale, undocumented barriers that also influence fine-scale wild boar movement in the real-world landscape.

#### Wild Boar Habitats Canton of Zürich
To facilitate and evaluate the transferability of the automated QGIS tool to the independent study area, the shapefile Potenzial_Wildschwein_Kerneinstaende_ZH_2024_WILMA.shp was incorporated into the methodology. This vector dataset was developed in December 2024 by the ZHAW Wildlife Management Research Group (WILMA), commissioned by the Canton Zürich Veterinary Office. The dataset spatially delineated potential core resting habitats (Kerneinstände) for wild boars across the entire canton, capturing the specific landscape structures required for daytime refuge and shelter.

The defining benefit of utilizing this dataset was its crucial role as a spatial validation reference during the tool's transfer phase. Because the empirical GPS telemetry data used to calibrate the resistance model was strictly limited to Canton Aargau, an independent biological baseline was required to test the automated pipeline's performance in Canton Zürich. This shapefile provided those necessary ecological anchors. It allowed for an objective evaluation of whether the QGIS plugin, applying statistical parameters strictly calibrated in Aargau, could accurately predict low-resistance pathways and functional connectivity corridors between these biologically relevant core patches in a novel landscape.

Regarding data quality, the dataset offered a high degree of regional specificity and ecological depth, having been explicitly developed for the topographical and infrastructural conditions of Canton Zürich by wildlife experts.

However, a fundamental limitation of this dataset was its predictive nature. It represented a potential habitat model derived from spatial parameters and expert criteria, rather than an empirical distribution map based on actual GPS tracking of wild boars currently living within Zürich. Consequently, while the dataset was highly effective for validating the tool’s spatial logic—confirming its ability to successfully connect highly suitable landscape patches according to ecological theory—it could not be used to confirm the actual physical presence or real-time movement of wild boars between those specific patches.

## Resistance Surface Pipeline
This section outlines the analytical framework utilized to model landscape permeability for wild boars. The overarching goal of this pipeline was to translate empirical animal movement data into a spatially continuous resistance surface at a 25-meter resolution. The methodological design was heavily adapted from established ecological connectivity frameworks, specifically integrating the analytical approaches detailed by Fischer et al. (2024), Clontz et al. (2021), and Keeley et al. (2016).

The computational workflow consisted of three primary sequential phases: the regularisation and hierarchical classification of raw GPS telemetry into distinct behavioral movement states, the empirical estimation of habitat preferences via an integrated Step-Selection Function (iSSF), and the mathematical transformation of these statistical coefficients into absolute landscape resistance values. All calibration and validation steps detailed in this section were initially prototyped and executed within the R programming environment. This ensured the statistical robustness and ecological validity of the baseline model before the entire algorithm was subsequently translated into the automated Python architecture of the final QGIS plugin.

### Telemetry Processing
The initial processing of the wild boar telemetry data was conducted entirely within the R programming environment, with all spatial geometries standardized to the LV95 coordinate reference system (EPSG:2056). To ensure the biological validity of the movement data, the raw GPS dataset was subjected to a rigorous cleaning protocol. All timestamps were standardized to UTC, and spatial validity checks were performed to remove erroneous coordinates. To eliminate behavioral anomalies associated with the collaring process, the first five days of tracking data for each animal (capture-shock period) were systematically dropped. Furthermore, any individual deployment containing fewer than 100 total GPS fixes or spanning less than 30 days was excluded from the analysis to ensure statistical robustness. One specific animal was entirely deleted from the dataset due to highly irregular and unreliable temporal intervals between fixes.

Following the initial cleaning, the continuous tracking data was converted into discrete movement steps using the amt (Animal Movement Tools) package. To standardize the temporal resolution for the Step-Selection Function, the trajectories were resampled to a consistent 15-minute interval, allowing for a 5-minute temporal tolerance. Because the raw data contained irregular interruptions and missing GPS fixes, the trajectories were split into continuous "bursts". Step lengths and turning angles were calculated exclusively within these bursts using the amt::steps_by_burst() function. This burst-splitting mechanism ensured that any temporal gap exceeding the 20-minute maximum threshold (15 minutes + 5 minutes tolerance) terminated the burst, preventing the algorithm from falsely calculating a spurious, massive step length across a data gap.
During this resampling process, all redundant secondary fixes recorded at sub-15-minute intervals were deleted. While this resulted in a nominal retention rate of approximately 60–70% for certain individuals (e.g., deployments 027_Agat_13969 and 039_Pete_12272), this represented an expected algorithmic deduplication of redundant data, rather than a biological data loss.

### Step Classification
Because a resistance surface is designed to model the energetic cost of traveling between habitats rather than foraging or resting within them, it was strictly necessary to isolate the movement data into two distinct behavioral states: in-patch (stationary/foraging) and in-matrix (active transit) steps.

The baseline methodology of this project was inspired by the red deer connectivity study by Fischer et al. (2024), which utilized a fractal analysis combined with k-means clustering and a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) to classify step behaviors. However, initial testing revealed that this specific clustering approach was biologically inappropriate for wild boars. Red deer exhibit highly distinct spatial separation between stationary behavior and large-scale seasonal migrations. In contrast, wild boars are highly resident; they generally remain within a defined home range and only undertake long, directed migrations when searching for a new social group, escaping severe disturbance, or reacting to drastic landscape alterations.

To adapt to this distinct ecological behavior, the complex GMM approach was discarded in favor of a targeted, rule-based classification system designed to isolate rapid, directed transit movements. Evaluated sequentially using a conditional case_when function, a step was classified as a relevant in-matrix transit step if it satisfied any of the following three geometric rules:

1. Absolute Distance: A single step length strictly greater than 250 meters.

2. Directed Travel: A single step length greater than 150 meters combined with a turning angle of less than $\pi/4$ radians, indicating highly directional, straight-line movement.

3. Sustained Travel: A sequence of three consecutive steps, all exceeding 100 meters in length and exhibiting low turning angles, indicating sustained, directed travel over a 45-minute period.

All remaining tracking data that did not trigger these rules—characterized by short step lengths and high turning angles—were classified as in-patch movements, representing localized behaviors such as resting, wallowing, or foraging. Only the isolated in-matrix steps were subsequently utilized to fit the resistance model.

### Spatial Covariates
Following the behavioral classification of the telemetry data, the environmental covariates required for the integrated Step-Selection Function (iSSF) were mathematically derived and standardized. All spatial layers were processed to perfectly align with the 25-meter LV95 master grid, utilizing the defined study area bounding box.

#### Forest Cover and Structure
Forest availability provides critical refuge, thermal cover, and foraging opportunities for wild boars. Consequently, forest cover and its spatial configuration were extracted from the land-cover dataset (tlm_bb_bodenbedeckung) within the swissTLM3D Geopackage. Three different Forest Layers were defined for the iSSF fitting. 

- **Binary Forest Cover:** Polygons representing forested habitats were filtered based on their specific semantic object types ("Wald", "Wald offen", "Gebueschwald", "Gehoelzflaeche") and rasterized into a binary forest mask (1 = forest, 0 = non-forest). During rasterization, a strict "all-touched" inclusion rule was applied, ensuring that any 25-meter pixel intersecting a forest polygon—regardless of the overlap fraction—was classified as forest. This methodological choice was essential to preserve narrow tree lines, hedgerows, and small copses, which frequently function as vital movement corridors and stepping-stone habitats for wild boars navigating predominantly agricultural landscapes.

- **Local Forest Density:** Because habitat selection is often driven by the broader landscape context rather than a single point location, a local forest density covariate was calculated. A circular moving window (focal matrix) with a 50-meter radius was passed over the binary forest raster. To ensure mathematical accuracy, particularly along the boundaries of the study area, the focal weights were converted into a strict Boolean mask. This allowed the spatial algorithm to calculate the exact mean value, representing the proportional forest cover (ranging from 0.0 to 1.0) within the immediate vicinity of every pixel. Ecologically, this covariate captured the structural density of the habitat, enabling the model to differentiate between sparse, fragmented tree cover and dense, continuous woodland blocks.

- **Distance to Forest Edge:** Wild boars exhibit a well-documented behavioral affinity for ecotones—the transitional boundaries between protective forest cover and open agricultural foraging grounds. To accurately model this behavior, a continuous "distance to forest edge" covariate was computed. For pixels located in open terrain, the Euclidean distance to the nearest forest pixel was calculated. Conversely, for pixels located strictly inside the forest matrix, the Euclidean distance to the nearest open, non-forest pixel was calculated to determine "forest depth". These two spatial gradients were then merged into a single, continuous raster layer. This specific metric allowed the spatial model to clearly differentiate between highly attractive forest edge zones, exposed open fields, and deep, isolated forest cores.





### Spatial Covariantes
After the Step Classification was done, the Study Area was defined and the Spatial Covariantes were loaded and prepared for the iSSF.

#### Forest
Forest availability and structure provide critical refuge, thermal cover, and foraging opportunities for wild boar. Therefore, forest cover and its spatial configuration were derived from the land cover dataset (tlm_bb_bodenbedeckung) within the swissTLM3D database.

##### Forest Cover
Polygons representing forested areas were filtered based on their object type (objektart == c("Wald", "Wald offen", "Gebueschwald", "Gehoelzflaeche")) and rasterized onto the 25-meter LV95 master grid to create a binary forest mask (1 = forest, 0 = non-forest). During rasterization, a strict inclusion rule was applied to ensure that any pixel touched by a forest polygon was classified as forest. This methodological choice was essential to preserve narrow tree lines, hedgerows, and small copses, which often function as vital movement corridors and stepping-stone habitats for wild boar navigating agricultural landscapes.

##### Local Forest Density
Because habitat selection is often driven by the surrounding landscape context rather than a single point, local forest density was calculated. A circular moving window (focal matrix) with a 50-meter radius was applied across the binary forest raster. To ensure mathematical accuracy along study area boundaries, the focal weights were converted into a strict Boolean mask, allowing the model to calculate the exact mean, representing the proportional forest cover (from 0.0 to 1.0), within the immediate vicinity of every pixel. This covariate captures the structural density of the habitat, differentiating between sparse, fragmented tree cover and dense, continuous woodland blocks.

##### Distance to Forest Edge
Wild boar exhibit a strong behavioral affinity for ecotones (the transitional boundaries between dense forest cover and open agricultural foraging grounds). To accurately model this behavior, a distance to forest edge covariate was calculated. For pixels in open areas, the Euclidean distance to the nearest forest pixel was calculated. For pixels strictly inside the forest, the Euclidean distance to the nearest open, non-forest pixel was calculated to determine forest depth. These two gradients were then combined into a single, continuous raster layer. Ecologically, this metric allows the spatial model to clearly differentiate between highly attractive forest edge zones, exposed open fields, and deep, isolated forest cores. 

Finally, all forest layers were strictly masked to the clipped study area boundaries to ensure perfect topological alignment with the terrain and hydrological covariates.

#### Slope and TRI
Slope (in degrees) and the Terrain Ruggedness Index (TRI) were calculated with terras terrain function and derived using the digital elevation model DHM25 (swisstopo) at a 25-meter resolution. Because the native coordinate reference system of the DHM25 is LV03 (EPSG:21781), the buffered study area bounding box was temporarily transformed into LV03 to crop the raw elevation data, thereby optimizing computational efficiency and reducing memory load.

Slope represents the maximum rate of change in elevation between a focal pixel and its eight surrounding neighbors. This metric quantifies the steepness of the terrain, which is a critical factor determining the energetic cost of movement and the overall physical accessibility of the landscape. To capture local topographic heterogeneity, the Terrain Ruggedness Index (TRI) was calculated. TRI computes the mean of the absolute differences in elevation between a central pixel and its adjacent cells. Ecologically, TRI serves as a quantitative measure of fine-scale surface roughness, it identifies sharp topographic variations, ravines, and highly uneven terrain that may function either as natural physical barriers or as sheltered micro-refugia.

Once the slope and TRI matrices were calculated on the unsmoothed, native-resolution surface, the resulting covariate layers were subsequently reprojected onto the master LV95 (EPSG:2056) study grid using bilinear interpolation. Finally, these topographic layers were masked to the exact, Swiss-clipped study area boundary to ensure perfect spatial alignment and extent matching with the other hydrological and infrastructural datasets.

#### Distance to Water
To model the distance to water, hydrological features were extracted from the swissTLM3D database (swisstopo). Instead of relying on the general land cover dataset (tlm_bb_bodenbedeckung), the dedicated hydrological layers (tlm_gewaesser_stehendes_gewaesser and tlm_gewaesser_fliessgewaesser) were utilized. The Bodenbedeckung layer aggregates various land cover types, but lacks the semantic depth in hydrological features required for high-resolution ecological modeling. Specifically, it does not provide explicit metadata regarding whether a river flows above ground or in a subterranean pipe, nor does it reliably distinguish fictitious lake axes from physical shorelines. Using the dedicated water layers allowed for precise attribute filtering and topological control necessary to accurately represent physical barriers and resources in the landscape.

Standing water bodies presented significant topological challenges, as the raw geometries were provided as 3-dimensional multilinestrings (LINESTRING Z) with fragmented shoreline segments. To accurately represent these features as solid physical barriers, a custom geometric reconstruction workflow was applied. First, the 3-dimensional Z-coordinates were removed to project all features onto a flat 2-dimensional plane, preventing algorithmic failures caused by minor elevation discrepancies along the shorelines. The dataset was then divided into true lakes (objektart == "See") and islands (objektart == "Seeinsel"). To resolve microscopic topological gaps in the swisstopo data, fragmented line segments were grouped by their unique Water Body ID (gwl_nr) and merged into continuous lines. These lines were then strictly cast into solid polygons, effectively forcing the closure of any remaining geometric gaps. Because islands represent passable terrestrial habitat, they could not be classified as water barriers. Therefore, the island polygons were geometrically subtracted from the primary lake polygons using a Boolean difference operation, resulting in highly accurate, solid lake geometries with intact terrestrial islands.

Flowing water was heavily filtered to reflect the ecological reality of wild boar movement. After dropping the 3-dimensional coordinates, a strict attribute-based filtration was applied. Only actual rivers and streams (objektart == "Fliessgewaesser") were retained, while fictitious water axes routed through lakes (Seeachse), dry channels, and industrial pipelines were excluded. Furthermore, the course of the river (verlauf) was filtered to retain only surface-level features (Oberirdisch, Brücke, Wasserfall). Underground rivers and piped streams (unterirdisch) were explicitly removed, as subterranean water flows do not represent physical barriers or drinking spots to terrestrial wildlife navigating the surface.

Finally, the highly processed, ecologically accurate vector geometries for both standing and flowing water were rasterized into a binary mask matching the resolution and extent of the master study grid. The Euclidean distance from every pixel to the nearest valid water feature was then calculated, establishing the final dist_water covariate layer for the habitat suitability and resistance models.

#### Infrastructure, Highway and Wildlife Passage Layers
The infrastructure component of the resistance surface captures the influence of anthropogenic linear features and built-up areas on wild boar movement. Wild boar exhibit strong but type-dependent avoidance of roads, railways, and settlements, and an accurate representation of these features, including a careful separation of barrier classes and the explicit removal of subsurface infrastructure, is essential for a behaviourally realistic resistance surface. 

All infrastructure layers were derived from the swisstopo SwissTLM3D 2026 vector dataset in the Swiss LV95 / LN02 reference system. Three feature classes were used: tlm_strassen_strasse for the road network, tlm_oev_eisenbahn for railways, and tlm_namen_siedlungsname for settlement polygons. Wildlife crossing structures were extracted from the federal Wildtierpassagen.gdb geodatabase (layer N2023_Version_Wildtierpassagen), and permanent African Swine Fever (ASF) protection fencing was taken from the Cantonal Veterinary Office of Zürich (Dauerzäune.shp). All vector data were loaded with a Well-Known-Text bounding-box filter set to the cantonal extent plus a 2 km quadratic buffer, ensuring that distance calculations near canton boundaries were not biased by edge effects from features just outside the study area.

SwissTLM3D stores all linear features as Polyline Z geometries. Since the resistance surface operates in two dimensions, and since several downstream operations — notably sf::st_buffer() and terra::rasterize() — are sensitive to or incompatible with Z- and M-coordinates, every loaded layer was reduced to pure 2D using sf::st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") immediately after import. A more substantive preprocessing decision concerned the removal of subsurface infrastructure. Wild boar do not perceive roads or railways that run through tunnels, underpasses, or inside buildings, and including such features as movement barriers would artificially fragment the resistance surface and bias the iSSF coefficient estimates. The SwissTLM3D specification provides two complementary attributes for identifying these features. The first, STUFE, is a numeric attribute encoding the vertical position of each segment relative to the surface, with values of -1 and -2 denoting first- and second-level underground passages respectively, and 0 denoting the at-grade default. The second, KUNSTBAUTE, is a categorical attribute describing engineered structures and includes the values "Tunnel", "Unterfuehrung" (underpass), "Unterfuehrung mit Treppe" (underpass with stairs), and "in/auf Gebaeude" (segments running in or on buildings). Rather than relying on either attribute alone, a custom helper function prep_above_ground() was implemented to apply both criteria sequentially: it first executes STUFE >= 0 as the primary numerically unambiguous filter, then applies a secondary string-based filter against the curated set of underground KUNSTBAUTE values. This redundant approach captures edge cases where one attribute is missing, inconsistently coded, or absent from particular features — for instance, building-internal road segments that are not formally classified as tunnels under KUNSTBAUTE but are flagged as STUFE < 0, and vice versa.

A second helper function, clean_railways(), was applied exclusively to the railway layer. This function removes segments flagged as out of service (AUSSER_BETRIEB == "Wahr"), as well as those identified as funiculars (STANDSEILBAHN), rack railways (ZAHNRADBAHN), or heritage lines (MUSEUMSBAHN). These specialty rail categories do not constitute typical fenced ballast-bed barriers and are either decommissioned, restricted to dedicated mountain alignments, or carry traffic so infrequent that they are functionally permeable to wildlife. Treating them as standard railways would overestimate the barrier effect of rail infrastructure in alpine and peri-alpine areas.

The OBJEKTART attribute of the road layer distinguishes 23 road categories ranging from motorways to alpine climbing routes. These were grouped into three ecologically meaningful classes reflecting the differential resistance imposed on wild boar movement. Fenced roads (FENCED_ROAD_CLASSES: "Autobahn", "Autostrasse", "Ausfahrt", "Einfahrt", "Zufahrt") represent the Swiss high-performance road network, which is comprehensively fenced under federal regulation; wild boar cannot cross these structures except at dedicated wildlife passages, and they were therefore treated as absolute barriers in the final resistance surface. Main roads (MAINROAD_CLASSES: "10m Strasse", "8m Strasse", "6m Strasse") correspond to multi-lane and wide single-lane primary roads carrying substantial through-traffic; they elicit strong avoidance responses in wild boar but are physically crossable. Secondary roads (SECONDARY_ROAD_CLASSES: "4m Strasse", "3m Strasse", "2m Weg", "Dienstzufahrt") cover narrower drivable roads, including residential streets, agricultural service roads, and the wider forest tracks.

Several OBJEKTART categories were deliberately excluded after careful evaluation of the specification. The category "Verbindung" is defined by swisstopo as a "virtuelles Verbindungsstück" — a virtual connector with no real-world physical presence, used solely to maintain topological network closure; including such virtual lines would introduce phantom barriers. The category "Platz" represents squares and parking areas, which are not linear features and are already captured by the settlement polygon layer. The categories "Autozug" and "Faehre" describe car-train and ferry transport routes — non-terrestrial conveyances that are not physical barriers on land. Finally, "Klettersteig" (alpine via ferrata), "Markierte Spur" (marked but invisible tracks), "1m Weg", "1m Wegfragment", "2m Wegfragment", and "Provisorium" were excluded as either non-existent on the ground, fragmentary, or provisional features that do not constitute consistent landscape elements.

Built-up areas were derived from the polygon layer tlm_namen_siedlungsname, filtered by objektart to retain the four settlement granularity classes: "Ort" (entire locality), "Ortsteil" (district), "Quartier" (neighborhood), and "Quartierteil" (sub-neighborhood). This polygon-based representation was chosen over the alternative tlm_bauten_gebaeude_footprint (individual building footprints) because wild boar respond to the contiguous built-up matrix — characterised by noise, light, human activity, and impervious cover — rather than to the geometry of individual structures. Distance to settlement edge therefore provides a more biologically meaningful predictor than distance to the nearest building, while also yielding smoother and computationally lighter distance rasters.

After class-based filtering, each road class, the railway layer, and the settlement layer were stamped onto the 25 m master grid using terra::rasterize() with touches = TRUE. The touches argument is critical for narrow linear features: it ensures that any pixel intersected by a road or railway centerline — regardless of fractional coverage — receives a value of 1. Without this flag, segments of roads thinner than one pixel diagonal can be silently dropped, fragmenting otherwise continuous barriers. For each thematic layer, a Euclidean distance raster was then computed using terra::distance(), which calculates, for every cell, the planar distance to the nearest cell of value 1. The resulting five distance rasters — dist_fenced_road, dist_main_road, dist_secondary_road, dist_settlement, and dist_railway — were subsequently masked to the cantonal extent and saved as intermediate GeoTIFFs.
This per-class distance representation, rather than a single aggregated "distance to any infrastructure" layer, allows the iSSF to estimate separate selection coefficients for each infrastructure type. This is methodologically essential because the four infrastructure classes have qualitatively different ecological signatures: a wild boar tolerates proximity to a forest service road but actively avoids motorways and settlements, and these contrasts are not detectable when the infrastructure types are pooled into a single covariate. In addition to the five distance rasters, a combined binary infrastructure mask r_infra was constructed for use in the resistance-surface burn-in step. It aggregates fenced roads, main roads, secondary roads, railways, and settlement polygons into a single layer marking every pixel directly occupied by any infrastructure feature. A separate binary r_highway raster was created from FENCED_ROAD_CLASSES alone, isolating the absolute-barrier subset for use in the final burn-in.

Wildlife crossing structures from Wildtierpassagen.gdb were transformed to the LV95 reference system, spatially filtered to the buffered cantonal extent, and buffered by 30 m to ensure that the entire crossing structure — including approach ramps and adjacent fenced corridors — was captured at the 25 m raster resolution. The resulting r_passages raster identifies pixels where wild boar can safely cross otherwise impermeable infrastructure. 

For Canton Zürich, an additional Zürich-specific barrier layer was constructed from the permanent woven-wire ASP fencing erected by the Cantonal Veterinary Office. Unlike ordinary agricultural fencing, which most ungulates can jump, ASP fences are explicitly designed to be wild-boar-proof. They were rasterised to r_fences_zh and masked to the canton, then treated as absolute barriers in the Zürich resistance surface.



The five per-class distance rasters enter the pipeline at two distinct stages. First, during iSSF fitting, values are extracted at observed and random step endpoints and z-standardised using the Aargau training mean and standard deviation. The standardised covariates dist_fenced_road_sc, dist_main_road_sc, dist_secondary_road_sc, dist_settlement_sc, and dist_railway_sc are then included as fixed effects in the conditional logistic regression, yielding selection coefficients β that quantify the relative avoidance or preference for each infrastructure type during directed transit movements. Second, during resistance-surface construction, the standardised rasters are combined into the linear predictor η using these β coefficients, transformed into a habitat-suitability raster S ∈ [0, 1] via min–max normalisation, and converted to a resistance raster R via the Keeley exponential transformation R = exp(C × (1 − S)) with C = 4. Finally, absolute-barrier pixels are burned in at R = R_max ≈ 54.6 (motorways, direct infrastructure pixels, ASP fences, and near-open-water at 0.9 × R_max), and wildlife passage pixels are burned in at R = R_min = 1, ensuring that connectivity analyses route freely through these crossings while avoiding impermeable infrastructure.
This two-tiered design — empirically estimated continuous avoidance gradients from the distance-based covariates, combined with hard-coded absolute barriers from the binary masks — reflects the biological reality that wild boar responses to infrastructure are continuous at intermediate distances but become categorical at the structure itself. It also ensures that wildlife passages, which would otherwise be invisible to the model because they affect connectivity rather than habitat selection, are correctly represented as low-resistance corridors in the final surface used for cantonal-scale connectivity modelling.

## QGIS Plugin





## Datensatz

Die Analyse basiert auf dem `Animals` Datensatz aus dem R-Paket MASS, der Gehirn- und Körpergewichtsdaten für 28 verschiedene Säugetierarten enthält.

### Datenquelle und Charakteristika

Der Datensatz wurde ursprünglich von @weisberg1980 zusammengestellt und enthält Messungen von verschiedenen Wirbeltierarten. Die Daten umfassen sowohl terrestrische als auch aquatische Säugetiere mit einem breiten Spektrum von Körpergewichten.

### Datenqualität und Limitationen

Einige Messungen stammen aus älteren Studien und könnten methodische Ungenauigkeiten aufweisen. Besonders bei sehr grossen Tieren wie Elefanten können die Gehirngewichte schwer präzise zu bestimmen sein.

## Statistische Analyse

Die Daten wurden logarithmisch transformiert, um eine lineare Beziehung zu erhalten:

```{.r}
log(Gehirngewicht) = log(a) + b * log(Körpergewicht)
```

### Transformationsverfahren

Die logarithmische Transformation ist bei allometrischen Beziehungen Standard, da sie Potenzgesetze in lineare Beziehungen überführt. Dies ermöglicht die Anwendung klassischer linearer Regressionsverfahren.

### Modellvalidierung

Die Residuen wurden auf Normalität und Homoskedastizität überprüft. Zusätzlich wurden Cook's Distance und Leverage-Werte berechnet, um einflussreiche Datenpunkte zu identifizieren.

## Visualisierung

Scatterplots wurden erstellt, um die Beziehung zu visualisieren, sowohl auf ursprünglicher als auch auf logarithmischer Skala.

### Graphische Darstellung

Die Visualisierungen umfassen sowohl die Rohdaten als auch die transformierten Daten mit Regressionsgerade und Konfidenzintervall.

### Software und Pakete

Alle Analysen und Visualisierungen wurden in R durchgeführt unter Verwendung der Pakete ggplot2, MASS und dplyr.
